USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Publish the final Section 301 list and impose the already-announced 25% tariffs on roughly $50 billion of Chinese goods targeted at aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery, and Made in China 2025-related lines. Do not accept Beijing’s weekend purchase package as a substitute for structural remedies on IP and forced technology transfer. Keep a negotiating channel open, but do not pause or roll back the $50 billion action again; do not widen to a much larger tariff tranche until China’s response is observed.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modest, not existential. The U.S. real economy is not yet paying a material trade-war tax: consumer sentiment is still firm (UMCSENT 98.2), industrial production is higher on the window, and VIX has settled near 13 after the May 29 announcement. Bilateral goods flows still show a large imbalance (IMPCH ~$44.5B vs EXPCH ~$10.9B in the latest month), which is the political and 301 predicate, not a recession signal. The threat that does exist is concentrated: China has a ready $50B retaliation list aimed at soybeans, autos, and aircraft, and farm-state pressure is already visible because China takes about 61% of U.S. soybean exports (~$12B). That is real sectoral and political exposure, but it is not a supply-chain or ally-cohesion crisis at this date. The deeper interest at stake is the unremedied 301 finding (22 Mar) that China’s IP/tech-transfer regime is unreasonable; the 8 Nov 2017 Beijing visit produced MOUs and no structural IP concessions, and the 19 May joint statement only promised larger purchases. Mnuchin called the war “on hold”; ten days later the White House correctly put 301 back on (29 May) because purchases do not fix the technology problem. Ross–Liu talks (2–3 Jun) reproduced that pattern: a reported ~$70B ag/energy/manufacturing buy if Washington drops tariffs, with Beijing stating that any outcomes die if the U.S. proceeds. That offer is leverage working, not a settlement. Implementing the teed-up $50B is therefore the proportionate next step — it converts the May 29 commitment into a credible bargaining chip rather than another bluff, and it is still far short of maximal escalation. The 7 Jun ZTE lifeline ($1B fine, board change, monitors) already spent a large non-tariff chip and drew bipartisan congressional blowback; stacking more entity-list/export-control escalation now would burn remaining non-tariff ammunition and complicate talks without fixing IP. Widening tariffs immediately would also raise the odds that China executes the soybean hit and that input-cost complaints from U.S. manufacturers (USTR hearings) become a broader CPI/political problem. Hold/negotiate-without-tariffs would recreate 19 May. Hence a modest positive threat reading (+0.20) and a moderate escalate-tariffs stance: do the $50B, demand structural movement, and wait to see whether Beijing retaliates or re-engages.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer findings remain unremedied after the Nov 2017 visit and the May 19 purchase-only statement
May 29 decision to proceed with 25% on ~$50B already teed up a June mid-month list; pausing again would make U.S. threats look reversible
China’s June offer of ~$70B ag/energy buys is explicitly conditioned on no U.S. tariffs and does not address SOEs, investment restrictions, or forced tech transfer
U.S. macro still healthy (sentiment, IP, low VIX); dispute has not yet produced a GDP-level hit
China’s matching $50B list targets soybeans/autos/aircraft; soy is a concentrated farm-belt vulnerability (~$12B, majority of U.S. soy exports)
ZTE denial order showed non-tariff leverage; the 7 Jun settlement already spent that chip amid congressional resistance, so further non-tariff escalation is the wrong instrument this week

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B), targeting aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery and related sectors.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft) in response to the Section 301 list.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment latest 98.2 (2018-06-01), still firm; no collapse in household confidence ahead of the tariff decision.
VIX 12.94 on 2018-06-13 after a brief jump to 17 on 2018-05-29; markets are not pricing an imminent U.S. financial-stress event.
U.S. goods imports from China still ~$44.5B in the latest month versus exports to China ~$10.9B (EXPCH); bilateral imbalance intact and not yet compressed by tariffs.

China offered to purchase nearly $70 billion of energy, agricultural and manufactured products in the first year if the U.S. suspends tariffs; the offer leaves untouched market access and forced IP transfer.
Beijing warned all talk outcomes will not take effect if the U.S. imposes sanctions including raising tariffs; White House still planning a final $50B list by June 15.
Trump could slap China with tariffs as soon as Friday; USTR had not yet published the formal 301 determination as of June 12.
Commerce deal to lift the ZTE ban for a $1 billion fine, leadership change, and U.S. compliance monitors, over objections from Republican lawmakers and some economic officials.
ASA: China buys 61% of total U.S. soybean exports and more than 30% of overall U.S. soybean production; a 25% soybean tariff is no longer hypothetical.
